Resolved by [PR 28](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/pull/28).

## Decision

- `Artifact` is the discriminated semantic subject; the initial discriminator is `kind: "typeShape"`.
- A `ReviewUnit` contains one root artifact and its finite recursive evidence projection. References are `expanded`, `included`, or `omitted`; the root is not its own reference, and a back-edge to it is `included`.
- One changed root produces one review unit and one logical Jev evaluation. Three roots produce three units and three logical evaluations.
- `SourceFingerprint` identifies exact captured source. `ReviewProjectionFingerprint` identifies the canonical semantic evidence projection. Observation/checkpoint identity does not belong on the review unit.
- `ChangeObservation` is raw host or reconciliation evidence. A `ChangeSet` exists only after complete stable capture; incomplete or unstable capture produces no change set and is represented by `ObservationResult`. Empty complete change sets are valid.
- `ReviewWorkItem` freezes one unit with its observation, change-set, rule-set, and input-contract context. Queue position and runtime state are not fields on the value.
- The backend vocabulary is `ReviewWorkItem -> ReviewInput -> ReviewResult`; `BackendResponse` is internal to evaluation. No separate rendered-input, backend-request, eligible-unit-set, or advice-delivery-item domain type is introduced without a distinct concept.
- Results aggregate into `AdviceBatch` for coherent host delivery. Work and result queues are transient, in-memory, nonpersistent, hard-bounded by items and retained bytes, and reject admission explicitly when full. Numeric limits and full-queue policy remain scheduling decisions.
- Transient review values may contain immutable source. Persistent reconciliation state remains source-free and regenerates unfinished work after restart.

## Evidence

The retained [contract](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/master/experiments/review-unit-vocabulary/contract.ts) typechecks independently. One explicitly authorized Effect `DecisionModel` / `@effect/ai-typesafe` validation call completed in 602 ms with zero retries. Eight rules remained below the configured advice threshold; the sole naming/type-width finding was addressed with distinct validated value types. No raw response, credential, source-bearing response, or individual probability was retained, and no post-correction paid call was made.

The canonical terms are recorded in the [domain glossary](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/master/CONTEXT.md).

## Restart-semantics correction

The restart statement in the resolution above is superseded by the decision made while resolving [Define the unified review-ingress and exact-snapshot deduplication contract](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/20).

Queues, cached review results, and pending review work are memory-only. A process restart may lose queued, running, or completed-but-undelivered work; the product does not reconstruct that work. Source-free checkpoint metadata may persist to compare complete observations across host-hook invocations, but it is not a durable work log and is not responsible for regenerating lost reviews. No source, rendered request, review unit, backend response, or advice is persisted by this checkpoint state.

This correction narrows restart guarantees; it does not change the vocabulary resolved by this ticket.

Work paused at a newly exposed prerequisite. [Research: Codex hook and product process lifetime](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/master/RESEARCH-CODEX-HOOK-PROCESS-LIFETIME-2026-09-20.md) establishes that pinned Codex 0.155.1 spawns a fresh child for every command-hook invocation, while `mcp_tool` hooks can call an already-connected MCP server. The repository had selected a one-shot command adapter for version one; it had not compared that product choice with a resident integration.

The decisions already reached here remain provisional inputs: direct and checkpoint observations converge at semantic admission; canonical logical Jev-request bytes define evaluation identity; queued/running duplicates join; completed successes use a bounded in-memory cache; failures never satisfy identity; mutation history is out of scope; restart may lose memory-only work.

Checkpoint persistence and cross-event cache/queue lifetime cannot be finalized until [Prototype resident MCP-hook lifecycle on pinned Codex](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/30) informs [Choose the product process lifetime and hook transport](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/31). This ticket is now blocked by that decision and is being released rather than resolved.

## Conformance result — ready for prototype review

The answer is **yes, once connected, for the tested headless invocation**. One resident MCP server received native `apply_patch`, Bash, and two Stop callbacks. The blocking Stop response caused the agent to return the requested acknowledgment in a completed assistant message. Command-hook observers had fresh PIDs per invocation.

Six live cases; **58/58 retained checks pass**. Boundaries:

- A six-second startup delay missed SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit; neither was replayed. Later edit/Bash/Stop callbacks arrived.
- Delayed replies, MCP `isError`, a crashed server, and a missing server allowed host progress. Later hooks did not restart the crashed server.
- No MCP SessionEnd callback arrived. Healthy servers received SIGTERM before the command SessionEnd observer; none survived host exit.
- Only pinned Codex CLI 0.155.1, Linux arm64, headless, stdio MCP was tested. No claim about concurrent sessions, HTTP, TUI/app-server, resume, or cancellation of server work.

Assets: [verdict and evidence](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/055df19/experiments/resident-mcp-lifetime/VERDICT.md), [runner and reproduction](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/055df19/experiments/resident-mcp-lifetime/README.md), [58-check ledger](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/055df19/experiments/resident-mcp-lifetime/checks.json). Captured on disposable branch `prototype/resident-mcp-lifetime`, based on master, in a separate worktree. No paid Jev calls or retained payloads/transcripts/credentials. No production implementation or architecture selection.

## Resolution

Completed the explicitly requested Luna Max research supplement, with parent review for evidence calibration. [Abide process and state lifetime review](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/843737e/RESEARCH-ABIDE-LIFETIME-2026-09-20.md) is captured on the separate `research/abide-lifetime-2026-09-20` branch.

Source inspection establishes:

- Claude Code and Codex install a fresh Abide hook worker per event; continuity lives in files under `~/.abide/sessions`.
- OpenCode adds a resident plugin map keyed by session, but still spawns the common worker for each event. Its map has no session-deletion cleanup path.
- Persistent keys use sanitized session/turn identifiers and omit host, repository/worktree, and agent identity. Claude can use the fallback `turn`; Codex documents parent session IDs for subagent hooks. Actual concurrent isolation/collisions remain untested.
- First-write files and marker counters address local parallel-hook races; they do not establish cross-agent/worktree isolation.
- Non-blocking Stop handling clears turn state. No Abide SessionEnd cleanup is registered; stale session pruning occurs at a later SessionStart after seven days. Source-bearing file state and Git snapshot objects have distinct retention lifetimes.
- Pinned and current lifecycle implementations are unchanged between the two inspected immutable revisions. Kimi Code and Pi are absent from the supported-host enum.

Advisory disposition: BORROW the adapter/common-worker separation and observation/backstop concept; REJECT copying source-bearing snapshots or insufficiently scoped state keys under the product's constraints. No dependency or product architecture was selected. All material findings separate SRC/DOC evidence from runtime verification; no live-host, concurrent-agent, or paid Jev run was performed.

The findings feed [Choose the product process lifetime and hook transport](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/31). Identity, cleanup, and recovery questions also fit the existing state/concurrency decisions; no additional duplicate tickets are needed.

Evidence inputs are now available:

- [Resident MCP lifecycle verdict](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/055df19/experiments/resident-mcp-lifetime/VERDICT.md): 58/58 checks across six retained cases; one resident server across edit/Bash/Stop, startup event gaps, fail-open errors/timeouts/crash, and shutdown before command SessionEnd. Prototype awaits its human review exchange.
- [Agent-host lifetime across hosts and concurrent sessions](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/commit/843737e): Luna Max source research, resolved as advisory. Fresh workers plus disk continuity; OpenCode resident map plus workers; explicit identity/cleanup/isolation gaps.

The decision remains open. Neither artifact chooses product architecture or persistence. Existing state/concurrency tickets cover the newly clarified implications; no duplicate frontier ticket was created.

## Discussion update — preference and recommendation, not resolution

The user prioritizes low-hassle Claude Code/Codex architecture, raised disk-preserved state plus a fresh process per call, and noted that queues can persist. SQLite is their current storage inclination, explicitly a separate technical question.

Recorded in [Agent-host architecture discussion](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/commit/cba2ace).

Recommendation: host-specific command-hook adapters, one common TypeScript/Effect worker, and source-free persistent state with transactional work claims and an advice outbox. This borrows a similar process shape without adopting source-bearing snapshots or a session-only state namespace.

A durable queue survives process exit but needs a running worker to advance. The unresolved behavior is whether work may wait for the next hook/explicit drain or must continue independently while the host is idle/gone. Exact-input recovery also cannot reconstruct old source from hashes if files change. SQLite, local user-state placement, identity partitioning, leases, and delivery receipts remain proposals to evaluate against that behavior.

This does not select an architecture, adopt SQLite, authorize implementation, or silently expand the map's pinned Codex supported envelope; Claude Code still needs a declared version and conformance surface.

## Confirmed user constraints

Ordinary edits let the agent continue; deliver coherent feedback at the earliest supported opportunity, with bounded turn-end collection. This was already established and should not be reopened as an unanswered preference.

The user explicitly accepts losing suggestions after a crash and wants recovery against current state. Guaranteed recovery/replay of pending reviews or completed-but-undelivered results is not required. The earlier fresh-worker + durable work/advice storage recommendation was provisional and is not accepted architecture.

This aligns with the existing [Define review scheduling and batched host-delivery semantics](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/23) constraints: in-memory nonpersistent work/advice queues, bounded count/bytes, restart loss permitted, explicit normal-operation queue-full policy. Do not introduce durability for crash protection of suggestions. Source-free checkpoint state is a separate concern.

Recorded in the [Research discussion supplement](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/commit/b738a2c). A lazily started resident worker with in-memory state remains a candidate. Host dispatch/lifetime/feedback research is still the prerequisite to choosing the process architecture; this comment does not resolve that decision.

## Resolution

[Hook dispatch, batch boundaries, and feedback delivery research](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/b4fc85d/RESEARCH-HOOK-DISPATCH-AND-FEEDBACK-2026-09-20.md) is complete, using Luna Max research and parent evidence review.

Command hooks create distinct per-invocation workers; hosts do not route later events to the latest-started worker. Sharing one in-memory reviewer requires an existing resident transport or product-owned IPC/ownership. Current Claude documentation describes a PostToolBatch boundary and per-tool parallel callbacks; this is documentation evidence, not pinned live Claude conformance. Async review completion and model feedback delivery are different boundaries, with host-specific delivery and teardown limits.

Retained pinned Codex runtime evidence demonstrates MCP residency across edit/Bash/Stop. Lazy ensure-running remains a product protocol to implement/test, not an MCP hook guarantee. The report names bounded probes for concurrent startup, event cardinality, feedback timing, and session/agent/worktree isolation.

The accepted behavior remains nonblocking ordinary edits, coherent feedback and bounded turn-end collection, in-memory bounded queues, and permissible crash loss. No durable queue/SQLite requirement or production architecture was selected. No new paid calls or host installations were made.

## Resolution

The human discussion has accepted the bounded finding that a resident process can own in-memory review state ("so we found that we can have in-memory state guy? that's good"). Crash loss is explicitly acceptable; recovery concerns current state.

The factual answer is yes for pinned Codex CLI 0.155.1 on Linux arm64/headless: one MCP server receives edit/Bash/Stop callbacks, with 58/58 checks passing. Startup gaps, lack of hook-triggered crash restart, and absent MCP SessionEnd delivery remain explicit limits. See the [retained verdict](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/055df19/experiments/resident-mcp-lifetime/VERDICT.md).

This closes the conformance prototype only. It does not select MCP over a product-owned resident worker or establish Claude runtime conformance. [Choose the product process lifetime and hook transport](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/31) is the next decision.

## Resume handoff — start here

The user is ending this conversation and wants to resume this decision tomorrow. This comment is the current session handoff; earlier fresh-worker/durable-queue recommendations are superseded proposals, not decisions.

### Settled — do not ask again

- Goal: useful, coherent feedback to the agent, with low operational hassle for Claude Code and Codex. Implementation mechanism is secondary.
- Ordinary edits let the agent continue. Deliver collected advice at the earliest supported opportunity, with bounded turn-end collection. Do not repeatedly ask whether to block every edit.
- Work/advice queues are bounded, in-memory, and nonpersistent, as already recorded in [Define review scheduling and batched host-delivery semantics](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/23). Bound both item count and retained bytes; normal queue-full handling is explicit.
- The user accepts losing suggestions after crashes. Recover against current state. Do not design guaranteed historical replay, durable queues, or an exactly-once recovery system to protect suggestions.
- Source-free observation/checkpoint persistence is a separate question. Source-bearing persistence remains out of scope. SQLite was an earlier inclination if storage is needed, not a requirement or selection.
- Each semantic review unit still gets an individual Jev request. Collecting advice does not combine semantic units into a backend request.
- A worker may remain alive and drain available work. The latest-started worker does not automatically own other invocations' work; host dispatch and product ownership are separate.
- The user prefers a background process with in-memory state IF it simplifies the architecture. They proposed initialization startup plus lazy ensure-running on subsequent hooks. This is a preferred candidate to examine, not a final transport/ownership choice.

### What is proven / researched

1. [Resident MCP verdict](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/055df19/experiments/resident-mcp-lifetime/VERDICT.md): pinned Codex CLI 0.155.1, Linux arm64/headless, stdio MCP, one process across edit/Bash/Stop; synchronous blocking response observed in completed assistant message. 58/58 retained checks. Early startup events may be missed, later hooks do not restart a dead MCP server, MCP SessionEnd is absent. Prototype is resolved after human discussion. This proves one residency option, not all proposed daemon behavior or Claude compatibility.
2. [Hook dispatch and feedback report](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/b4fc85d/RESEARCH-HOOK-DISPATCH-AND-FEEDBACK-2026-09-20.md): Luna Max source/docs research completed. Ordinary command hooks spawn separate processes; no automatic routing of later events to an earlier worker. Claude current docs describe PostToolBatch; exact live Claude conformance remains untested. Async completion does not guarantee immediate feedback delivery; host checkpoints/teardown differ.
3. [Agent-host lifetime and discussion](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/commit/b738a2c): Claude/Codex use fresh workers plus on-disk turn state; OpenCode adds resident map but still launches workers. No review daemon or demonstrated durable task queue. Host/worktree/agent isolation and cleanup gaps are source-inspected/unknown, not runtime failures. Its source-bearing state is not a product template.

The research and MCP prototype tickets are closed. This process-lifetime decision remains open and will be unassigned for the next session.

### Next discussion and proposed probe

Compare two concrete resident options against the settled feedback behavior:

- Host-managed MCP server and MCP hook calls.
- Small command-hook clients forwarding to a product-owned resident reviewer over local IPC, started at initialization and lazily ensured on later hooks.

Specify only what is necessary to make that comparison testable:

- **Ownership/scope:** one reviewer per host session, per worktree, or shared across sessions with explicit routing? Who ends it, and what happens if no shutdown callback arrives?
- **Readiness:** how simultaneous initial hooks ensure one owner; startup deadline; stale endpoint handling; lazy restart with accepted state loss.
- **Delivery:** which hook/checkpoint returns pending advice; how ordinary edits return promptly; bounded Stop collection; avoid duplicate/stale or wrong-agent delivery.
- **Burst behavior:** several overlapping edits, one multi-file tool call, concurrent hook clients, one reviewer, bounded work/advice state. Per-host event cardinality is not yet fully runtime-proven.

## Resolution — command-hook clients with an idempotently ensured resident reviewer

The user accepted command-hook clients forwarding to a product-owned resident reviewer and explicitly proposed declarative, idempotent startup from hooks. They delegated ownership and readiness details to the simplest design, requested idiomatic TypeScript/Effect, reaffirmed that crash loss is allowed but normal-run suggestion loss is not, and clarified that the tested envelope must not become a permanent product restriction.

### Selected process boundary

Use short-lived host-specific command-hook clients and a resident product reviewer reached over local IPC. Initialization may eagerly ensure the reviewer exists; subsequent hooks perform the same idempotent ensure-running operation. Startup must not depend on observing initialization.

Use one reviewer per explicit agent-host session and canonical worktree pair as the simplest initial isolation boundary. Include host identity in the namespace; never infer ownership from whichever hook ran most recently. Separate sessions do not share queues. A hook client's exit does not end the reviewer or cancel work it has accepted.

Ordinary edit hooks return promptly after bounded admission and may return an available advice batch through the host's response format. The reviewer continues accepted work in memory. Later supported hooks collect pending advice; Stop performs bounded collection. Each semantic review unit still has its own Jev request.

### Readiness and lifetime

Ensure-running means connect to the existing matching owner or atomically establish one owner when absent. Concurrent hook invocations must converge on that owner. Use a bounded readiness deadline and bounded retries for genuinely transient startup races; exact values and OS mechanism are prototype details, not arbitrary product requirements. An IPC timeout alone is not evidence that the reviewer is dead and does not authorize replacing it.

Use the project's exact Effect RC cohort and ordinary scoped services/layers, resource finalizers, supervised worker fibers, and bounded retry schedules. Scope review work to the reviewer lifetime, not an individual IPC request. Effect's in-process coordination does not itself supply cross-process ownership; the IPC adapter must establish that.

Idle cleanup may stop an empty reviewer. It must not discard queued/running work or undelivered advice during an ordinary session pause. Explicit session termination requests orderly shutdown; a missing callback must not be treated as proof that a merely quiet host is gone. Exact final-delivery, host-gone detection, and interrupted-delivery behavior remain in the existing scheduling and concurrency decisions below.

### Loss boundary and correction to the preceding recommendation

Crash loss of in-memory queues, in-flight work, caches, and completed-but-undelivered advice is accepted. A later hook can start a fresh reviewer and recover against current state. No durable review queue, historical replay, or source-bearing persistence is introduced. Checkpoint persistence remains a separate decision.

The previous recommendation to discard work on an ordinary startup/IPC deadline or indiscriminately on idle restart is superseded. Accepted work remains owned by the live reviewer when a client times out or exits. Admission failure must be visible as unavailable/incomplete, never silently treated as reviewed. Normal-operation capacity, delivery, and shutdown must not silently lose suggestions.

### Design scope and evidence

The product remains host-neutral, with Claude Code and Codex as design targets. Codex CLI 0.155.1/Linux arm64/headless is the current validation baseline, not a literal architectural restriction. Add interactive/headful Codex to planned conformance testing and record it separately until tested. Other hosts require their own evidence before support is claimed.

The existing MCP prototype proves that alternative's residency properties; it does not validate the selected IPC design. Extend the existing unified-pipeline prototype to test the selected process boundary. No additional prototype is needed to choose the direction today, and no production implementation is authorized by this decision.

## Resolution — shared semantic admission and memory-only evaluation reuse

The process-lifetime prerequisite is resolved. The user accepted the resumed contract, requested that backend switching not complicate this design, and agreed that returning to previously reviewed contents may reuse a still-cached successful evaluation when the complete review input matches.

### Unified ingress

Dedicated direct-edit observations and checkpoint reconciliation converge at the same semantic admission boundary. Both use the established stable-capture, change-set, review-unit, and review-work-item vocabulary. An incomplete or unstable capture is an observation outcome, not evidence of successful review.

Keep exact source/snapshot equality distinct from review-projection equality. A path having appeared in a direct-edit event does not suppress a later different snapshot discovered at a checkpoint. Path, tool name, observation origin, and event ID alone are not evaluation identity. An unchanged root source alone also does not establish equality of its supporting evidence or complete review input.

The evaluation equality criterion is the canonical logical Jev-request bytes: the complete semantic input and rule content actually presented for evaluation. Observation/checkpoint IDs and transport bookkeeping do not make equivalent requests different. Source and projection fingerprints provide equality evidence; neither may substitute for equality of the complete logical review request. Distinct snapshots remain eligible for processing, while identical resulting review requests may reuse an evaluation.

Use one configured review backend for this contract. Dynamic agent/backend switching and a general backend-configuration identity framework are out of scope. A future backend change can invalidate the cache; no switching machinery is required here.

### Idempotency and reuse

Within the resident reviewer selected by [Choose the product process lifetime and hook transport](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/31#issuecomment-5754545125):

- An equivalent queued or running request joins the existing logical evaluation.
- An equivalent completed successful evaluation may be reused while retained in a bounded in-memory cache.
- An absent or evicted cache entry permits a new evaluation. This is bounded reuse, not an unbounded exactly-once guarantee.
- Failures and rejected admission never satisfy successful-review identity. Accepted work remains owned by the live reviewer if a hook client exits or times out.
- Each distinct semantic review unit is evaluated individually; units are not combined into a batch Jev request.

The scope follows the existing reviewer boundary: one agent-host session and canonical worktree pair. No shared cross-session cache or durable evaluation history is introduced. Restart may lose work, results, and cache entries under the accepted crash-loss boundary. Checkpoint metadata is not a durable review-work log.

### Concrete cases

1. A direct-edit hook and a checkpoint observe the same complete review input: join pending work or reuse its retained successful evaluation.
2. A later edit at the same path produces different review input: it remains eligible for a new evaluation.
3. A type changes from `name: string` to `name: string | null` and is then restored to `name: string`: the restored version may reuse its earlier successful evaluation if the complete review input matches and that result remains cached. Otherwise evaluate again.

Reusing an evaluation does not erase the new observation or itself decide whether advice should be delivered again. Mutation-history reconstruction is out of scope.

## Resolution — bounded resident-memory observation baseline

The user rejected filesystem and SQL persistence for checkpoint comparison, explicitly accepted restart coverage loss in exchange for leaving the filesystem untouched, required graceful bounded degradation rather than process failure, and accepted the simplified per-file artifact-projection model after two architecture reviews.

### Lifetime and scope

The product keeps exactly one current **observation baseline** in the resident reviewer, with at most one candidate reconciliation scan in progress. It keeps no checkpoint history and writes no checkpoint, artifact-index, review-work, result, or advice state to disk.

The reviewer already has one explicit agent-host-session/canonical-root scope. Within that process the root is simply its fixed canonical filesystem path; the observation baseline needs no Git worktree identity, branch, remote, model-provider identity, PID, or additional session key. Git may still affect file selection if the separate file-selection decision adopts Git ignore semantics, but it does not identify checkpoint state.

Reviewer restart discards the observation baseline. The first subsequent complete, stable reconciliation seeds a new baseline without reviewing every existing file and without refusing operation. Changes made before that seed may never be reviewed; this coverage gap is explicitly accepted. A live change to the resolved file-selection policy likewise starts a fresh baseline rather than comparing different eligibility regimes.

### Source-free comparison state

For each eligible file, the observation baseline retains:

- its normalized path and exact file fingerprint; and
- a bounded per-file collection of `ReviewProjectionFingerprint` values for the currently extracted artifacts.

It retains no source text. Initial baseline creation extracts those fingerprints locally but makes no Jev requests.

When a file fingerprint changes, the product transiently extracts its current artifacts and recomputes their projections. Only current artifacts whose projection fingerprint is new or changed become review units. Unchanged artifacts in the same file do not produce Jev requests. A file containing one hundred definitions can therefore be parsed locally while an edit to one definition produces one review unit.

A separately retained cross-checkpoint `ArtifactId` and per-artifact `SourceFingerprint` are unnecessary. Artifact identity may exist transiently while constructing one review unit's reference graph, and exact source fingerprints may exist transiently for stable capture and request correlation. The observation baseline retains only the file fingerprint and per-file projection fingerprints. Projection comparison must preserve the distinguishing root context and duplicate multiplicity; it is not a set of bare source hashes.

The complete logical Jev-request bytes remain the equality criterion for joining or reusing evaluations. Rule-set, input-contract, and other evaluation-scenario identity belong to that request/cache key, not to the observation baseline.

This decision keeps the already-deferred boundary from the declaration-extraction research: it does not select an unchanged root in another file merely because one of its dependencies changed. Deletion review semantics also remain out of scope.

### When the baseline advances

A file's new fingerprint and artifact projections are remembered once every review unit selected from that change has been handed to live review handling, joined equivalent pending work, reused an eligible successful result, or determined to require no review. The product does not wait for Jev to finish.

If required work cannot be accepted, the earlier file state remains remembered so a later checkpoint can retry. An incomplete or unstable observation produces no change set and never partially publishes a clean baseline. Accepted work may still be lost if the resident reviewer crashes, under the already-approved crash-loss boundary; no durable replay is introduced.

### Bounds and graceful degradation

Crossing a bound never crashes the product or blocks the agent merely because reconciliation is large:

- Evicting a completed successful review result is safe and may cause an additional Jev call.
- Evicting optional artifact-projection comparison entries is safe only when absence means `unknown` and therefore permits conservative re-extraction/review; absence never means unchanged.
- The exact per-file baseline is not silently made partial while claiming complete reconciliation. If enumeration, stable capture, time, file-count, or retained-byte bounds prevent a complete comparison, the observation result is incomplete, the prior complete baseline is retained, and direct-edit observations continue normally.

Exact supported numeric limits belong to prototype measurement and the later supported-envelope decision; the existing 1,000-file measurement is evidence, not a semantic cliff at file 1,001.

### Required validation

The existing unified-pipeline prototype must validate this state model at three levels:

1. Pure/property tests over generated sequences of baseline seeds, complete/incomplete scans, file and artifact changes, cache eviction, admission success/failure, and policy reset.
2. Deterministic Effect tests for concurrent same-key work, cache success/failure/expiry, out-of-order scans, direct-edit/scan races, bounded admission, and stale-generation rejection without sleeps.
3. A real temporary-filesystem test with a TypeScript file containing roughly one hundred definitions: seed without backend calls, change one definition, assert one review unit/fake-backend call, then assert zero calls for an unchanged checkpoint. Include unstable reads and bounded/incomplete recovery.

Use the pinned Effect cohort. `effect/Cache` fits bounded successful-result reuse but must not own the authoritative observation baseline; the latter needs explicit atomic state. Strict pending-work joining must not rely on cache eviction behavior that can evict an in-flight lookup. No third-party cache dependency is selected.

This resolves a planning decision only. No production implementation, prototype execution, filesystem persistence, or paid Jev call was performed.

## Resolution — finite dispatch cycles and retained, bounded advice

The user accepted finite cycles, completion-or-age advice collection, retained over-budget advice, and explicit admission rejection. They chose the simple restored-snapshot behavior and clarified the lifetime boundary: return whatever feedback is ready at turn end without denying completion; losing all remaining work/advice when the agent application closes is acceptable.

### Dispatch and collection

- When idle, a lone due review item starts promptly, without waiting for a quota or batching delay. Capture currently ready work as a finite dispatch cycle; arrivals after its selection belong to a later cycle. Continuous arrivals cannot extend one cycle indefinitely.
- Each review unit still gets its own logical Jev request. This decision does not choose concurrency numbers, parallelism topology, backend request batching, truncation, or huge-change scaling.
- Completed results enter the bounded result/advice store. For ordinary delivery, collect results until the cycle completes or its maximum advice-wait time expires, whichever comes first. Later completions remain eligible for subsequent collection; new arrivals do not reset the oldest pending result's wait.
- Deliver eligible results through the earliest supported subsequent command-hook reply. An eligibility timer does not manufacture a host delivery opportunity. Ordinary edit hooks remain prompt and do not wait for newly accepted evaluations to finish.
- Turn-completion/Stop collection is bounded and may flush the ready subset even while its cycle or other reviews remain unfinished. Return one useful advice batch within the response budget; do not withhold available feedback, require queue quiescence, or deny/extend agent turn completion merely to finish reviews. Any operational unfinished status accompanies available feedback, rather than replacing it or implying a clean review.

### Admission, memory bounds, and ownership

The resident reviewer owns admission, queued/running evaluations, and retained results independently of any individual hook/IPC request. A client timeout does not cancel accepted work or clear advice.

Both logical queues are memory-only, bounded by hardcoded item and retained-byte limits. Admission must account for queued/running inputs and reserve bounded space for promised retained outcomes before accepting new work. Reservations must use enforceable size bounds, not assume unknown backend output fits. A failure to admit is explicit and incomplete, never silently accepted or reported as reviewed. Already accepted work remains owned by the reviewer. This does not introduce source-bearing spill storage.

Preserve one globally budgeted advice response per hook interaction; the existing default finding budget of five applies to the combined response, not separately to each unit or cycle. Excess eligible advice remains pending for later responses rather than being dropped by the formatter. Selection must be deterministic and allow older eligible advice to progress. Bound response bytes as well as retained queue bytes; operational status does not bypass the response size bound. Disabling advice through a zero finding budget must not be reported as successful advice delivery.

The asynchronous admission/retained-advice behavior supersedes the old synchronous PostToolUse-only delivery behavior and needs a versioned successor adapter contract in the final specification. It preserves the globally budgeted single-response shape and non-denial behavior. It does not establish new host conformance claims.

### Evaluation reuse is separate from current advice

Keep a bounded, memory-only successful-evaluation cache, with count and retained-byte limits. Cache pressure may evict successful evaluations and cause later re-evaluation; failures are not reusable successes. No unbounded delivered-history registry is required. Exact capacities and optional expiry tuning belong to the prototype and supported-envelope decision.

Equivalent pending requests join the same accepted evaluation independently of cache eviction. Joined observations of the same current input do not multiply advice. Pending advice is retained independently of the cache; evicting a reusable evaluation cannot silently evict its pending advice.

For A → B → A, where A and B are different applicable review inputs:

1. Observing B retires stale pending advice for A. Late A completion must not publish advice that no longer applies.
2. A's successful evaluation may remain cached.
3. Restoring A may reuse that evaluation and make its advice eligible again, even if A's advice was delivered before B. If evicted, evaluate again.

Retirement follows actual applicability, not any unrelated edit in the same file. Detailed stable-capture, generation, and delivery-race handling remains in the existing concurrency decision. Routine stale retirement is an explicit relevance transition, not silent capacity loss.

### Turn end, pauses, and actual session termination

A turn-end hook deadline limits that collection attempt; it does not mean the agent application has closed. Remaining accepted reviews continue and completed advice stays in the second queue for later hooks. Ordinary pauses, IPC timeouts, and idle cleanup must not discard this state while the session is alive.

**When the agent application actually closes, all remaining work and advice may be discarded.** Crash loss is also accepted. There is no requirement for an explicit collection command, post-exit reviewer retention, guaranteed final drain, or historical replay. This supersedes the broader normal-shutdown retention wording in this ticket and the earlier process-lifetime decision. A quiet host alone is not evidence of closure.

Returning bytes over IPC is not proof of model-visible delivery. Keep uncertain delivery outcomes honest; this does not require crash recovery or an exactly-once protocol. The existing concurrency decision owns evidence of host closure, delivery handoff, and uncertain outcomes under this simpler loss boundary.

## Resolution — attributable direct-event truth with bounded, lossy recovery

The live discussion resolved this ticket. The product may lose events, review work, results, cache entries, and advice when capture is uncertain, capacity is full, backend attempts fail, or the resident reviewer restarts. It must not turn loss or uncertainty into a clean result, and it must not publish corrupted or mixed review data.

### Direct-event boundary

The default Codex direct-edit observation is a successful `PostToolUse` event for native `apply_patch` in the validated Codex CLI 0.155.1 envelope. `Edit` and `Write` are matcher aliases; the observed tool is still `apply_patch`. The hook payload contains host/session/turn/tool identity, `cwd`, and a Codex patch command with `Add File`, `Update File`, or `Delete File` headers. The event supplies candidate paths and attribution evidence, not authoritative final file bytes or a universal changed-line set. A pure rename/move, metadata-only change, arbitrary shell write, or external write is not claimed by this direct-event contract. `Bash` is not a direct-review event because its payload does not provide a reliable resulting path set. `Stop` and checkpoint reconciliation belong to [Decide checkpoint reconciliation coverage and mechanism](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/38), not this map.

The Codex host adapter translates this envelope into the host-neutral direct-edit observation. The core pipeline does not parse Codex patch text. The canonical observation must carry the host-provided advice recipient/agent identity and canonical working root; it must preserve subagent identity and never infer ownership from the latest caller or from root co-location alone.

### Capture and source truth

The product's `SnapshotReader` reads the current eligible file from the filesystem after the direct event. The event does not supply the final source. The chosen capture policy is the conservative Q1-A boundary: use Effect-scoped capture facilities to read and hash the path conservatively, with agreement checks for repeated reads/metadata. If a path changes during capture, is missing, is non-regular, or cannot be captured stably, do not create a `ReviewUnit` for that path; report an incomplete or skipped outcome if an outcome is exposed. Never admit mixed or partial bytes as a clean review. Paths in one multi-file observation may produce independent outcomes; an unstable path does not make another stable path's bytes valid or invalid.

A `Snapshot` is transient evidence for one capture boundary. It is not a backup, mutation history, or durable replay record.

### Work data structure and algorithm

Use Q2-A: one singleton resident reviewer when that is the simplest process boundary, with in-memory state partitioned by `(advice recipient, canonical working root)`. Keep:

- a bounded FIFO work queue;
- a bounded result/advice queue for each recipient/root partition; and
- a `Map` of queued or running work keyed by the complete logical `ReviewInput` identity for one `ReviewWorkItem`.

A duplicate logical request joins queued/running work. A distinct snapshot is distinct work. A fixed worker bound limits concurrent backend calls. Full item/byte bounds reject admission explicitly. There is no required debounce window and no latest-wins replacement policy. This is bounded throttling, not an exactly-once system.

Each semantic `ReviewUnit` remains an individual Jev evaluation. A completed result enters the bounded advice path only while it remains applicable to its intended recipient/root.

### Late results and freshness

Use Q2b-A. Before advice delivery, re-read and re-extract the current `ReviewUnit` when the implementation can establish that identity. Compare the complete logical `ReviewInput` or its `ReviewProjectionFingerprint`, not only the whole-file hash. If an unrelated interface or artifact in the same file changes, an earlier result may remain applicable. If the reviewed artifact/evidence changes, the result is `stale` and cannot be delivered as current advice.

A stale result is not automatically retried. A later direct event creates new work organically. If that later event is lost or rejected by bounds, losing the recommendation is allowed. If artifact-level identity cannot yet be proven, the implementation may fall back to a conservative whole-file comparison and lose more advice; it must not claim unaffected advice is current without evidence.

### Truth and loss vocabulary

Use Q3-A: a few truthful boundary outcomes, not one mandatory global status enum or a permanent end-to-end record for every event. A `ChangeObservation` says an edit may have happened. A `ChangeSet`/`ReviewUnit` exists only after stable evidence. A `ReviewResult` means one actual work item obtained a valid backend result. An `AdviceBatch` is a host delivery attempt. `incomplete`, `unavailable`, `rejected`, `stale`, and `expired` are never clean evidence. “No findings” requires a successful review with adequate evidence. Without reliable acknowledgement, delivery means submitted to the host, not seen or acted on by the model.

Pending advice may expire by its configured relevance age and may be discarded. No durable replay, exactly-once guarantee, acknowledgement tracking, delivery retry system, tombstone history, or status endpoint is required. Best-effort bounded diagnostics remain optional.

### Restart and recovery

The accepted Q4 boundary is actual restart or loss of the resident reviewer process, not a hook-client timeout by itself. If the reviewer is still alive, accepted work remains owned by it. If it really restarts, in-memory queued work, running work, cached successful results, and pending advice may be lost. The new reviewer starts with empty work state; no durable replay is required. The implementation may discard whole work items, but it must never publish a partial `ChangeSet`, mixed-recipient result, invalid `ReviewResult`, or advice for the wrong snapshot/recipient. Bounded cleanup is allowed only after work, advice, and resources are gone. No post-exit collection, final drain, or model-visible delivery proof is promised.

This resolves a planning decision. It authorizes no production implementation; the disposable prototype and supported-envelope decisions validate the contract separately.

## Resolution amendment — Q5 clarified and contract audited

This amendment supersedes the earlier resolution wherever that text allowed a whole-file freshness fallback or treated a projection fingerprint as sufficient identity. The ticket was reopened for this audit and is now resolved with the following bounded direct-event contract.

### What the MVP actually reads

The MVP does not create Git worktrees and does not require users to use them. A worktree is an already-existing checkout directory; if one exists, its canonical root is a separate identity for consent and internal partitioning. It is optional isolation evidence, not a product feature or writer lock.

“Current root” means the canonical working-tree identity resolved from the event's `cwd`; it does not mean “scan the whole repository again.” A direct event names candidate paths. Capture reads only those paths, possibly repeating content/metadata reads to establish a stable capture, then extracts the relevant `ReviewUnit`. Before advice handoff, it revalidates only the relevant path/unit and its supporting evidence. Checkpoint-wide scans belong to issue #38.

### Q5 — same-artifact overwrite before first capture

Codex's direct hook supplies path/recipient evidence and the patch command, but no authoritative post-image bytes or hash. If agent B replaces A's same artifact before the first product read, two matching reads establish what the product saw, not that A produced it. A separate `memfs` snapshot does not solve this: its snapshot utilities recursively serialize/restore a filesystem-like tree and provide no transaction boundary or writer identity. `Effect` supplies scopes, cancellation, retries, queues, and serialized state; it does not provide an atomic arbitrary-filesystem snapshot.

The strict, simple rule selected by the user is therefore:

- do not send an A-specific recommendation when the captured unit cannot be established as A's edit;
- do not reinterpret B's current bytes as A's review;
- a later direct event from B may create its own review organically; there is no hidden self-retry;
- if the race is invisible to the available evidence, the MVP does not claim exact attribution under that unsupported concurrent-writer envelope. It must not turn path plus matching reads into a false attribution.

There is no whole-file fallback. If a semantic unit's identity or supporting evidence cannot be established, that unit is unavailable/skipped; an independently stable unit may still proceed without making the parent multi-file observation a complete `ChangeSet`.

### Capture, identity, scheduling, and publication

- Stable capture is conservative and Effect-scoped. Unstable, missing, non-regular, or malformed paths do not become clean evidence. A declared deletion is skipped/out of scope; a recreated path is not treated as the deleted output. Unsupported move syntax is skipped rather than reading the wrong path.
- Freshness compares the independently identified `ReviewUnit` and complete canonical logical `ReviewInput`, including rule content and relevant input-contract context. A projection fingerprint is evidence only when it covers that complete identity; a different file snapshot can still yield the same logical request.
- One singleton resident reviewer is acceptable when simplest, with explicit recipient partitioning by host/session/agent as needed and canonical root. A child is never redirected to its parent merely because they share a root. Failed or uncertain IPC is attempted/unacknowledged, not delivered.
- Work uses bounded keyed FIFO state. Duplicate logical requests join before new capacity is reserved; queued/running joins are protected from cache eviction. Dispatch has finite cycles and starts the first item promptly. Successful-result reuse is bounded. One combined advice response is selected deterministically; advice overflow is retained subject to bounded admission rather than silently discarded by formatting. Count and byte limits apply globally as well as per tenant, including capture/extraction and duplicate bookkeeping.
- Capacity failure is explicit at admission. Accepted fresh outcomes are not arbitrarily evicted. Stale retirement, relevance expiry, backend failure, cancellation, malformed responses, admission rejection, or reviewer restart may lose work/advice. Backend failures never satisfy successful-review identity.
- Revalidate relevant source, rules, and input-contract evidence at publication. This can suppress known superseded results but cannot promise freshness after handoff.

### Recovery and truth boundaries

A real resident-reviewer restart may lose all in-memory work, cache, results, and pending advice; no durable replay is required. A hook timeout alone does not cancel reviewer-owned work. New reviewer state rejects obsolete lifetime messages. Cleanup releases reservations and join entries on every terminal path. Loss remains allowed, but mixed bytes, mixed recipients, partial `ChangeSet`s, invalid review results, and stale advice must never be published as clean/current.

This resolves the direct-event planning decision. It authorizes no production implementation. The filesystem-snapshot research is retained in [RESEARCH-FILESYSTEM-SNAPSHOT-2026-09-21.md](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/main/RESEARCH-FILESYSTEM-SNAPSHOT-2026-09-21.md); `memofs` was not investigated because `memfs` was conclusive.

## Resolution — permissive named-path selection, Git-ignore defaults, and analyzer-owned applicability

The live discussion resolved this ticket for attributable dedicated direct-edit observations. This is a planning decision, not production implementation authorization.

### Direct-event selection

A trusted direct-edit observation supplies candidate file paths, so direct-event selection does not walk or recursively expand the filesystem. A directory-valued candidate is skipped without traversal. The built-in default is declarative and permissive: candidate paths are included unless an applicable exclusion rejects them. There is no hard-coded language or extension allowlist in file selection. Users may narrow the selected set with repository-relative include/exclude globs; accumulated product exclusions win over inclusions.

The product honors repository and nested `.gitignore` files using standard Git pattern and nesting semantics. It does not load `.git/info/exclude` or a global `core.excludesFile` in this milestone. Git ignore applies as Git normally defines it: tracked files remain eligible even when a pattern matches; ignored untracked paths are skipped. Opting ignored source back in is postponed rather than inferred from an ordinary include. Non-Git roots are unsupported in this milestone.

Excluded content must not be read or submitted for review.

### Mandatory safety floor

The following gates always win over declarative includes:

- the candidate must resolve to a regular, nonsymlink file inside the canonical Git working-tree root;
- Git administrative paths are never captured;
- `.env` and `.env.*` basenames are never captured;
- any path under a `node_modules` segment is always excluded — better safe than sorry; and
- selected input remains subject to bounded capture and the supported text/binary preflight.

Names such as `build`, `coverage`, `dist`, `generated`, `target`, and `vendor` are not universal exclusions. A direct event already names a path, so permitting such names does not imply scanning those trees. Users own the cost of deliberately broad declarative policy within global and per-partition byte/item/concurrency bounds.

### Selection is not semantic applicability

File selection answers whether a candidate path may be captured; it does not decide which programming language the path contains. After stable bounded capture, analyzer applicability determines whether content yields reviewable `Artifact`s and `ReviewUnit`s. The core therefore must not reject `.rs`, `.txt`, or another suffix through a global extension policy, and configuration cannot add or remove languages merely by naming an extension.

Each analyzer must contain its own applicability/probing and parsing behavior. It may use path, extension, bounded bytes, or parsing as private evidence. If no analyzer applies, or an analyzer contains a parse/applicability failure, no backend work or agent-visible advice is produced. These ordinary cases consume no advice tokens; bounded local diagnostics may record them. One file's failure does not suppress independently valid files.

The shared boundary protects analyzers from obvious binary input with bounded capture, supported text decoding (including an accepted UTF-8 BOM), and NUL rejection. There is no universal semantic test for malformed or unsupported content: beyond that narrow preflight, analyzers own applicability and must treat arbitrary bounded input as untrusted without escaping failures.

### Checkpoint follow-through

These direct-event semantics do not authorize a catch-all filesystem walk. Checkpoint reconciliation needs a separate discovery/traversal decision, likely with allowlisted discovery and safe pruning, while reusing the same declarative configuration vocabulary. That concern is carried into the checkpoint-reconciliation map rather than solved here.

## Resolution — validated within a narrow candidate envelope

The live prototype discussion resolved this ticket after the user authorized bounded paid Jev validation and directed the work to continue through the full pipeline.

### Verdict

Yes: the disposable prototype validates the resolved direct-event contract for attributable, controlled-writer, named TypeScript direct events on the recorded Codex CLI 0.155.1 / Linux arm64 / headless surface. It does not establish production readiness or support outside that envelope.

The retained prototype is on [`prototype/direct-event-pipeline`](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/tree/prototype/direct-event-pipeline), ending at [`76b6139`](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/commit/76b6139). The complete [verdict](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/76b6139/experiments/direct-event-pipeline/VERDICT.md) and [reproduction guide](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/76b6139/experiments/direct-event-pipeline/README.md) are the primary context.

### Evidence

- The deterministic offline suite passes 21 scenario groups covering selection with zero reads for exclusions, repeated stable capture, independent multi-file outcomes, malformed/nonregular/missing paths, writer uncertainty, semantic identity, pending joins, successful reuse, failure non-reuse, stale retirement, capacity, expiry, response bounds, recipient/root isolation, process ownership, timeout, crash loss, cleanup, and lazy restart.
- A 100-caller startup stress converged on one owner; eight separate client processes found that same owner.
- [The provider-seam milestone](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/76b6139/experiments/direct-event-pipeline/evidence/live-jev.json) made exactly two paid Jev calls with zero retries. Expected clear and finding bands passed at 321.3 ms and 321.6 ms.
- [The complete resident-pipeline milestone](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/76b6139/experiments/direct-event-pipeline/evidence/live-pipeline.json) made exactly two paid calls with zero retries after real event adaptation, capture, extraction, admission, and before semantic publication revalidation. Both units were admitted; full-rule evaluation took 466.7 ms and 289.0 ms; the clear unit emitted no advice and the finding unit emitted one advice item after an unrelated comment changed the file.
- [The initial resident attempt](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/76b6139/experiments/direct-event-pipeline/evidence/live-pipeline-initial-rejected.json) is retained because an unresolved `Date` reference correctly stopped the clear fixture before admission. It consumed one valid finding call, no retry, and led to a self-contained corrected fixture.
- The paid extension consumed five calls total across the provider-seam run, the initial resident attempt, and the corrected resident run. No retry was issued. Retained evidence excludes source, credentials, raw responses, advice text, individual probabilities, and provider usage.
- [The final pinned headless host run](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/76b6139/experiments/direct-event-pipeline/evidence/host-run-1790035254066.json) observed native edit admission with no immediate advice, then one advice item submitted on the next Bash hook. The model did not repeat it, so the result is truthfully `attempted-unacknowledged`, not claimed model-visible delivery.
- The TypeScript check passes. Ordinary tests remain deterministic and offline.

### Candidate envelope and limits

The affirmative verdict is limited to explicit Codex session/agent identity, canonical Git roots, controlled-writer fixtures, named event paths, bounded UTF-8 input, and uniquely named TypeScript interface/type units with finite same-file evidence. Invisible same-artifact overwrite remains unsupported because stable reads do not prove writer identity. Cross-file/schema extraction, hard Node/native RSS accounting, interactive Codex conformance, real child-specific delivery, and Claude Code conformance remain unestablished.

The recorded count/byte/worker/advice/expiry values are experiment parameters for [Set the initial supported envelope from prototype evidence](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/issues/26), not requirements selected here. The supported-envelope decision owns which of these claims and limits become normative.

This closes a disposable prototype decision. It does not authorize production implementation.

## Research resolution

[Secure local credential storage for Codex onboarding](https://github.com/dearlordylord/jevs/blob/4c60514e46b372ad9a5cb3a820cabb83592cae02/PRODUCT-RESEARCH-ADVISORY-2026-09-22-CREDENTIAL-STORAGE.md) records primary-source evidence, candidate classifications, dependency gates, and prototype acceptance checks. Source branch: `research/onboarding-credential-storage`.

Native stores can support the intended pattern, but headless Codex within a logged-in user session and a server without a session vault are different support profiles. Source inspection does not establish actual Codex/macOS access.

- Linux Secret Service provides explicit locked/prompt semantics. macOS has distinct file-based and data-protection Keychain implementations; packaging and executable identity affect access.
- `@napi-rs/keyring` 2.1.0 is a conditional candidate, not an adopted dependency. Its default Linux fallback uses reboot-volatile keyutils; persistent onboarding must explicitly select Secret Service.
- The wrapper exposes no public macOS no-prompt option, and its async API does not prove cancellation of an in-flight native operation. Prompt suppression, bounded failure, and package/update behavior require a native spike.
- Replacement/logout must target the owned item, distinguish absence from failed deletion, and account for resident reviewer caches. Environment injection remains an explicit automation alternative, not a substitute for enter-once storage.

No paid calls, real credential access, keychain mutation, package installation, or macOS execution occurred. The research question is resolved as advisory facts and unresolved runtime checks; no user choices or production support gates are marked complete.

## Resolution — terminal-first CLI, agent-callable setup, install once, explicit updates

The user accepted the terminal setup approach and user-scope installation with separate repository enablement. They additionally requested that the coding agent be able to invoke the CLI and clarified that update notices are optional if simple; updating itself is required.

- Provide an installed CLI as the first distribution/activation surface. A native Codex plugin is deferred, not a prerequisite. Exact public package/executable naming and packaging artifacts remain release details; npm is a proposal rather than a newly adopted dependency decision.
- Install once for the user's selected Codex configuration home. Enable review separately for each canonical repository/backend/destination. Installation never grants source-egress consent.
- Support agent-initiated setup, diagnosis and updates using the same CLI: explicit parameters, noninteractive operation, structured outcomes and repeatable/resumable steps. This is an extension of the already-needed headless interface, not a second architecture. The usability/runtime details must be validated in the walkthrough.
- Do not route raw API keys through agent conversation or command arguments. Where user secret entry, vault unlock, host trust or unresolved consent is necessary, report a bounded actionable user step instead of hanging or bypassing the boundary. Existing concrete user authorization remains usable; no redundant confirmation requirement is introduced.
- Run a durable installed version from hooks; do not resolve/download a package on every edit. Preserve other tools' configuration and remove only owned integration entries.
- Updates are user-requested. Provide an update command. Update-available notices are optional only if inexpensive/simple; omit them rather than add a notification subsystem. No automatic background upgrades. Actual update failures and host-required trust/restart steps must still be reported truthfully.
- Use the ordinary host trust flow, retaining the distinction between configured, trusted, enabled and observed review. Agent invocation does not require or justify relaxing host permissions.

The accepted target remains interactive/headless Codex on Linux/macOS. Clean-package installation, native parser/resident portability, agent invocation, native trust, credential access, other-hook coexistence, update/removal and real first review remain acceptance gates. Existing Linux headless evidence is not evidence those new gates have passed.

## Resolution — one saved key, explicit environment override, logout without losing repository enablement

The user accepted all three proposed defaults and delegated routine subsequent choices to the agent, reserving material scope, authority, or user-experience questions for discussion.

- Save one default Jev API key per user on a machine, shared by enabled repositories. Repository enablement remains separate. Multiple saved accounts and per-repository vault profiles are deferred.
- A supplied environment credential overrides the saved key without modifying it. Preserve explicit credential-variable selection; an explicitly selected missing or invalid variable must not silently switch accounts. Diagnostics identify the source, never its value.
- Logout forgets the saved key and stops new provider requests using that saved credential, including accepted-but-not-yet-dispatched work. Preserve repository enablement. A later login restores credential access without repeating repository consent. Requests already sent cannot be recalled, and local logout does not revoke the key at Jev.
- If an environment credential remains active, say so clearly; logout cannot erase the parent shell's environment. Repository disable remains the way to stop future dispatch there regardless of credential source.

Routine defaults selected under the user's delegation:
- Enter/save through a masked user-controlled login flow; an agent-operated noninteractive CLI reports the required user action rather than asking for the secret in chat.
- Use persistent native storage, with no plaintext or reboot-volatile fallback. Linux Secret Service and macOS Keychain are candidate platform mechanisms. No Node binding is adopted until its native no-prompt, deadline, packaging and real-host gates pass.
- Only explicit login/setup may interact with an unlock prompt. Hooks, resident review and offline doctor must not prompt or hang; report locked, absent, inaccessible and timed-out storage distinctly and preserve completed edits. Servers without an accessible native vault may explicitly use environment injection.
- Replace only the product-owned saved item; failed/cancelled replacement retains the old usable key. Successful replacement/logout invalidates the saved credential generation in resident/queued work before later dispatch.
- Report failed deletion honestly, never as successful logout. Prevent further use of the saved credential while logout recovery is pending; explain whether the vault item still remains. Do not delete other tools' credentials.
- Saving a key does not prove backend validity or grant source-egress consent. Paid verification remains a separately requested, bounded demo; ordinary setup diagnostics make no review call.

## Current #105 idea and worktree map — 2026-09-25

**Architecture under discussion.** Treat the agent-to-Jev-to-agent path as event-driven data flow. One attributed edit admits an ingress job to the resident's existing work queue; preparation may put multiple review-unit jobs into that same queue. An eligible unit produces an Effect `DecisionModel` request to Jev and receives a separate response event. A finding becomes resident-owned pending advice; clear and unavailable outcomes stay distinct. Background and Stop are collection opportunities over that same advice, not extra review queues or reasons to rerun Jev. Collection grants a lease for a bounded delivery batch. A completed hook write is host submission; model visibility and repair require separate observation. The agent's repair is a new edit observation.

The owner-approved next design is to **reoffer at Stop** when background submission is recorded but model consumption is unknown, and to put collection policy, leases, submission state, and Stop reoffer behind a cohesive host-neutral resident delivery API. Those choices are in the issue body. They are **not yet implemented** in the candidate branch and do not waive the remaining Linux race, isolation, failure, and timing gates.

The [Foldkit visualization package](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/tree/prototype/issue-105-agent-flow/packages/agent-flow-viz) is a separate, provisional sidecar. Its typed transition table is used by both its reducer and chart; each data arrow has an event, location, and data flavor. It models one recipient and one review unit so we can discuss the event boundaries. It is not wired into the installed product, does not derive from production code, and is not host or Jev validation evidence. Run it with `cd packages/agent-flow-viz && npm install && npm run dev` from its branch.

Vocabulary update: the owner prefers **agent round** for one request to one agent through accepted completion or cancellation. Clarification of native `decision: "block"`: the agent runtime calls Hapsland's Stop hook **after the agent tries to finish and before the runtime accepts that finish**. Hapsland can return `{"decision":"block","reason":"..."}`. Here “block” means **do not finish yet**; the runtime presents the reason to the agent and continues its work. Hapsland does not issue a separate restart command. The candidate's next Stop returns quietly. The number of Stop continuations and any final drain/cancel policy remain open owner decisions.

Owner clarification, 2026-09-26: **waiting inside a synchronous Stop hook** holds the finish decision while Hapsland collects advice. It is not the native `decision: "block"` response. That response is sent only after the wait if Hapsland chooses to prevent completion and give advice to the agent; the round then remains active. If Hapsland allows Stop and the agent runtime accepts completion, the round ends.

The owner directs that an ended round leave **no data that can trigger another review or delivery for that round**. #105 now requires round-scoped closure of admitted observations, queued capture/review jobs, running Jev work, pending advice/notices, leases, background waiters, submitted/uncertain records, and Stop state. Late admission and completion callbacks must be fenced; cancelled/discarded work must be reported as incomplete, never clean; other rounds must be unaffected. The candidate contract states these as [five candidate formal properties](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/blob/feat/issue-105-composed-delivery/docs/issue-105-composed-delivery.md#round-close-cleanup-direction) at [`b1c8f13`](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/commit/b1c8f13). Current production code has no round-scoped cancellation/closure path.

One boundary remains to establish: Hapsland knows the result of its own Stop hook, but that alone may not prove the runtime accepted completion when other Stop hooks also run. #105 asks for an observable closure boundary or an explicit limitation. The number of Stop continuations remains an open owner decision; cleanup applies when the round actually closes.

### Stop terminology and diagram clarification

The Foldkit diagram in [draft PR #108](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/pull/108) now uses **“Advice receipt time unknown”** for its grey band. `Stop`/`SubagentStop` is the agent runtime's finish-attempt hook. Hapsland can wait inside it. **Observed current profile.** `src/resident/capacity.ts` supplies one shared canonical ledger with 512 items / 64 MiB globally and 16 items / 2 MiB per partition; `src/canonical/adapter.ts` currently rejects larger item caps. `Dispatch.bend` has one eight-running-job cohort shared by preparation and evaluation today; #148 explicitly splits this into an eight-job preparation bound and a distinct eight-active-Jev-call permit pool. `Round.bend`, `DeliveryState.bend`, and `Canonical.bend` repeat the four-continuation decision. `ImportGraph.bend` embeds 256 KiB/file, 20 KiB/tree, eight files, 1.5 MiB reads, 16 outgoing edges, depth four, and 128 work steps. **Expose the following bounded settings, preserving their present defaults:**

| --- | --- | --- |
| `stopContinuationsPerRound` | Integer **0–4**, default **4**. Zero permits finish with no Hapsland-requested continuation; 1–4 permit at most that many additional continue-with-advice opportunities in one Hapsland round. These are authorizations, not guaranteed model-visible turns or repairs. Do not raise the default or ceiling without new host evidence. | User maximum; project may only lower it. | Four resident ledger caps | Positive integer items: global 1–512, partition 1–16; byte caps: global 1–64 MiB, partition 1–2 MiB. Require each partition cap ≤ its matching global cap. Defaults remain 512/64 MiB and 16/2 MiB. | Optional local user resource caps, with project policy allowed only to lower. Snapshot at resident start; a cap change requires draining/restarting the resident. Pass the effective value once to canonical Bend initialization. |
| `preparationJobs` and `jevCalls` | Separate integer 1–8 settings, each default/ceiling 8 **after #148 lands**. No combined “dispatch concurrency” knob. | Resident-start snapshots. Bend decides job admission and Jev permit issuance independently; native code executes only commanded effects. A lower Jev pool still uses #148's immediate-unavailable saturation behavior until #139 defines waiting. |
| Graph budgets | #142 should expose positive finite effective limits for per-file source (≤256 KiB), accepted encoded tree (≤20 KiB), files (≤8), total reads (≤1.5 MiB), outgoing edges (≤16), depth (≤4), and work steps (≤128), using those values as current defaults. Bend alone chooses accept/skip/read/terminal using it; native capture enforces a physical pre-read ceiling. #138 supplies the cross-file capture path. |

# Python source-review coverage research

**Purpose:** Identify a Python analysis profile and measurement plan capable of testing the user's goal of covering at least 90% of intended review use cases.
**Audience:** Product and specification owners, contributors including coding agents, and evaluation reviewers.
**Status:** Advisory research and bounded source-inventory evidence, 2026-10-09; no Python adapter implemented.
**Authority:** Product-specification advisory material; the accepted type/function review and runtime contracts remain authoritative. Inventory execution establishes counts, not Hapsland behavior.
**Expected use:** Decide a Python profile and build a coverage prototype using pinned source and edit cases; do not advertise 90% coverage from these results.

## Research brief and change log

Question: which Python roots, imports, packaging layouts, annotations and framework patterns must Hapsland understand to serve typed AI applications and their backend code? Date: 2026-10-09. This is the Python vector of the user's explicitly requested Python/Go research. It expands the language ranking with use-case inventory, not a new ranking or a product requirement.

Assumptions: Hapsland observes completed valid source edits and offers rule-controlled review through its existing runtime-neutral pipeline. It must preserve source capture, privacy/exclusions, freshness and omissions across advisory post-edit, optional blocking, multiple runtimes, headless operation and Jev failure. Runtime adapter correctness is a separate acceptance dimension; Python syntax does not alter that contract. The baseline is the existing adapter seam plus a maintained Python grammar, rather than building a parser or running the application's Python interpreter to discover symbols.

Discovery: official Python language/typing/packaging specifications, tree-sitter-python release source, Pydantic documentation, and six purposively selected public repositories. Search terms included `tree-sitter-python releases`, Python import/namespace/TYPE_CHECKING specifications and typed AI state. Include Python source under AI frameworks, an AI application, an AI gateway and a backend application template; exclude notebook cells and numeric kernels from this first pass because they need different source/edit identities, not because their users are irrelevant. Generated and utility files can remain in the broad inventory. A focused subsample removes repository tooling and FastAPI migrations by explicit prefixes. Source inventory is bounded at these six repositories plus official specs; it is not ecosystem saturation or a representative sample. Next discovery must add independent AI application teams and user edit traces.

Evidence that overturns the proposal: intended-user edits dominated by unannotated dictionaries, notebook state, ORM descriptors or dynamic schemas; framework source counts failing to predict application roots; more than 10% irreducibly dynamic bindings; packaging costs or parser version gaps preventing required host support. The proposed profile must then expand or the target audience must be explicitly reconsidered, without relabeling failures as covered.
